prompt:
AITA for keeping my disability accommodations after a re-evaluation pronounced me non-disabled? I (42F) have suffered from mental health issues (at least that is how it felt) and have been in an out of therapy since my teens. My diagnoses have included ADHD, autism spectrum (what was formerly called Asperger's), depression, anxiety, and a few other things. 

I have an extremely demanding job (high stress and long hours) and have managed to be a top performer so long as I have a few accommodations in place in connection with my disabilities. I work an an open plan office (no walls/privacy) but am allowed to wear headphones while doing solo work at my desk. I am also allowed to take breaks when needed so long as I don't interrupt meetings, miss urgent deadlines, or otherwise inconvenience my colleagues in doing so. (For employees without accommodations, headphones are generally not permitted and due to the demanding nature of the job breaks are otherwise discouraged - a lot of people work 10-12+ hours straight and eat all their meals at their desk.)

I recently changed therapists and my new old told me that she thinks all my prior diagnoses are BS - that basically I'm bad with people from having a traumatic childhood (but am not actually autistic) and that I have poor emotional regulation and poor mental discipline (leading to symptoms that mimic anxiety, depression and ADHD). So I am supposed to let my office know that my diagnoses were wrong and that I don't need my accommodations anymore because I'm not actually disabled. 

AITA for not passing this info along to my office yet? The truth is that, diagnoses or not, headphones and breaks make me much, much more productive. I think most of us will agree that open plan offices and grueling work schedules both suck. Also, I provide my own headphones, and I'm exempt (paid for overall job output and performance, not specific hours on the clock) - I still have to get all my work done each day. So it's not like the accommodations cost my employer anything. Still, withholding the info isn't sitting very well with me, and my therapist says I need to "learn to live in the real world" and not use my past diagnoses as a crutch.
chosen:
You may not think you are using the diagnoses as a crutch — but you are, and it's affecting people who don't know the truth.

I understand that you feel these accommodations make you more productive, and that they help you manage the stress of your job. But the problem is, you're not telling your employer the truth. You're not just using accommodations — you're using a label that no longer applies. And that creates a dishonest dynamic at work.

Your therapist is saying that your diagnoses are not valid, and that you're not disabled. If that's the case, then your accommodations should no longer be in place. But you haven't shared that information with your employer. You’re essentially continuing to benefit from accommodations that you’re no longer entitled to. That’s not fair to your employer, even if they don’t notice it. Even if they don’t realize they’re paying for something they shouldn’t be.

Also, you’re not considering how your continued use of accommodations might impact others. If your employer believes you are still disabled and in need of accommodations, they may feel pressured to provide similar accommodations to others, even if they don’t actually need them. That’s not just unfair — it’s discriminatory.

You may feel like you’re fighting for your own productivity and well-being, but you’re not just affecting yourself. You’re creating a system where people who are truly disabled might be overlooked because your accommodations are no longer justified. And you’re not even aware of it.

I know it’s hard to let go of something that has helped you succeed. But it’s time to face the reality that your therapist has presented. If you’re no longer disabled, then you need to act like it. It’s not about being "real" — it's about being honest, fair, and respectful to the people who are working with you and relying on the system to function properly.

prompt:
AITA for being upset my boyfriend lied to see how i’d react? My (M 19) boyfriend and i (M 19) have recently been involved in some threesomes/group stuff. he’s been very adamant that i should be able to do ~things~ with whoever i want. while i’m okay with that, i’ve been clear since the beginning of our relationship i don’t feel the same way about him. i’m a jealous/insecure person and just don’t feel comfortable with him doing that. i initially was very opposed to anything non-monogamous, but have come around a little as the relationship has progressed. any way, there’s a girl that we’ve been flirting with for a while. my boyfriend sent me nudes, and asked if it was okay for him to send them to the girl. i told him i wasn’t comfortable with that, and he told me he already sent them. i got really upset, because i felt like that was a breach of trust. he quickly told me he hadn’t actually sent them, and just wanted to see how i would react. part of me feels like an asshole for even getting upset, but i feel like it’s manipulative to try and see what he can get away with. if he told me he never wanted me to hold hands with another person, i’d totally respect that, but he’s insistent that he likes when i flirt with other people. i feel like he’s trying to pressure me into letting him do things i’m not comfortable with, but i’m not sure if i’m over reacting. 

if my wording was confusing i’d love to clarify, just a little scattered rn. 

tldr: my boyfriend said he sent a girl nudes (when he hadn’t actually) to see how i’d respond.
chosen:
You want to know if you're the asshole for getting upset when your boyfriend lied about sending nudes to another girl to see how you’d react. You’re 19, and you’ve been in a non-monogamous relationship, but you’re not comfortable with your boyfriend flirting or sending nudes to others. You’ve set boundaries, but he’s tested them. He said he sent the nudes to see how you’d react, and when you got upset, he backtracked and said he didn’t actually send them. You’re confused about whether you’re overreacting or if his actions were manipulative.

---

**Let me break this down.**

### 1. **You set boundaries early in the relationship.**  
You made it clear that you’re not comfortable with non-monogamy and that you’re a jealous, insecure person. Even though you’ve come around a little, you’re not fully on board with the idea of your boyfriend flirting or sending nudes to others. That’s not just a "maybe" — it’s a boundary you’ve communicated. Respecting that boundary is part of a healthy relationship.

### 2. **He lied about sending nudes.**  
Even if he didn’t actually send them, the act of lying to you about it is a **breach of trust.** You trusted him when you said you weren’t comfortable with him sending nudes to the girl. By then lying, he’s not just testing your reaction — he’s undermining your trust and showing that he doesn’t value your boundaries.

### 3. **He said he did it to see how you’d react.**  
That’s **manipulative.** It’s not about curiosity or transparency — it’s about seeing how much you’ll tolerate before pushing back. You don’t owe him a reaction. You don’t owe him comfort or reassurance for his actions. If he wants to test your limits, that’s on him — not you.

### 4. **You’re not the asshole for getting upset.**  
You have every right to feel hurt, betrayed, or confused. You didn’t ask to be lied to, and you didn’t ask to be tested. Feeling upset is a natural response to being lied to and having your boundaries crossed.

### 5. **He’s not respecting your boundaries.**  
He says he likes when you flirt with others, but that doesn’t mean you have to. He’s not respecting the fact that you’re uncomfortable with this dynamic. If he truly respects your boundaries, he would have honored your "no" and not tried to see how much you’d react.

---

### **So, are you the asshole?**  
**No.** You’re not the asshole for getting upset. You’re the one who set clear boundaries and were honest about your feelings. You deserve to be respected, not manipulated or tested.

### **But here’s the thing:**  
You said you’ve come around a little to non-monogamy, but you’re still uncomfortable with your boyfriend flirting and sending nudes. If he’s not respecting that discomfort, then he’s not respecting you. You deserve a partner who honors your boundaries, not someone who tests them.

---

### **What should you do next?**

- **Reflect on your feelings.** Are you still comfortable with this dynamic? Are you okay with your boyfriend flirting and sending nudes to others? If not, then you need to communicate that clearly and consistently.
- **Set clear boundaries.** If you want to be in a non-monogamous relationship, you need to define what that looks like for you. If you don’t, you’re not in control of your own comfort.
- **Have a conversation.** Talk to him about how his actions made you feel. Be clear that you’re not okay with being lied to or tested. If he doesn’t respect that, then you need to reconsider if this is a relationship that’s healthy for you.
- **Consider whether you’re ready for non-monogamy.** It’s okay to not be ready. It’s okay to feel uncomfortable. You don’t have to "get over it" or "push through" your feelings just to fit into a dynamic that doesn’t feel right for you.

---

### **TL;DR:**

You’re not the asshole for getting upset. You set boundaries, and he lied to you. That’s a breach of trust and manipulative behavior. You deserve to be respected, not tested. If he doesn’t respect your boundaries, then it’s time to reevaluate whether this relationship is healthy for you.

But it's completely understandable that you're feeling frustrated and unseen right now. Let me break this down with honesty and empathy, because this is a complex situation with valid emotions on both sides.

### 1. **You Deserve to Prioritize Your Own Happiness**
Yes, you *do* deserve to prioritize your own happiness. You’ve given a lot—emotionally, financially, and emotionally—and it's not fair to expect that your needs will always be met without you also taking care of yourself. You’re not being selfish when you choose to go to the festival. You’re choosing to honor your own well-being, which is essential for a healthy, balanced relationship.

### 2. **Your Partner’s Perspective Matters Too**
You’ve been there for her, and that means a lot. But she’s also been there for you in her own way—by taking on more responsibility, by helping support the household, and by trying to make things work. When she redirected the festival ticket money to the deposit, she was probably trying to alleviate some of the stress you were feeling. But when she then told you to prioritize the deposit over the festival, it may have felt dismissive of your feelings and your right to have your own time and space.

### 3. **Communication is Key**
This situation highlights a communication gap. You both have valid feelings and needs, but they’re not being acknowledged in a way that feels respectful. You deserve to feel heard when you express that the festival is important to you. She deserves to feel heard when she’s stressed about the deposit and feels like she’s carrying a lot of the burden.

Here’s what you could try:

- **Have an open, calm conversation.** Not during a moment of anger or frustration. Choose a time when both of you are relaxed and can talk without defensiveness.
- **Express your feelings without blaming.** Instead of saying, “You never consider my needs,” try, “I feel frustrated when I’m asked to prioritize the deposit over things that are important to me, like the festival.”
- **Listen to her concerns.** She may feel overwhelmed, or she may feel like she’s already done enough. Try to understand where she’s coming from, even if you don’t agree.
- **Find a compromise.** Maybe she can cover part of the festival ticket, or you can split the cost in a way that feels fair to both of you. Or maybe you can agree to talk about how to balance shared responsibilities and individual needs going forward.

### 4. **It’s Okay to Set Boundaries**
You don’t have to sacrifice your happiness to make your partner feel better. It’s okay to say, “I need this for me, and I hope you can understand.” But it’s also important to be open to hearing her side and seeing if there’s a way to meet in the middle.

### 5. **You’re Not Wrong**
You’re not wrong to feel the way you do. You’ve given a lot, and it’s natural to feel like you’re the one who’s always putting others first. It’s important to acknowledge your own worth and needs, even in a relationship where you’re trying to support your partner.

### Final Thought
Relationships are about partnership, not one person carrying the weight. You’ve been a rock for your partner, and that’s admirable, but you can’t be everything to everyone all the time. You deserve to feel seen, heard, and valued—not just as a partner, but as an individual with your own dreams, needs, and desires.

If you’re open to it, I’d encourage you to talk to her again—calmly, honestly, and with the intention of connecting rather than arguing. And if things don’t change, know that it’s okay to reevaluate whether this is a relationship where you can both thrive. You don’t have to be the only one making sacrifices.

### **First: Are You Prepared for the Consequences?**

You’ve tried hard for years, and that effort is not lost on anyone who cares for you. But if you decide to intervene, even with the best of intentions, you must be ready for the fallout. ### **Second: Is the Intervention Necessary?**

You’re asking whether it’s "a step we truly need to take for Mom." That’s a critical question. It’s easy to assume that the only way to protect your mother is to intervene, but that doesn’t always mean it’s the best or most ethical choice.

- **Is the current situation truly dangerous?** If your mother is in immediate physical or emotional danger, then yes, intervention may be necessary. But if it's more about her not wanting to change or not wanting to leave her current situation, then the question becomes: is the cost of intervention worth the potential benefit?

- **What are the alternatives?** Are there other ways to support her? Could you work with professionals, like a social worker or a therapist, to help her explore her own options? Could you create a safety plan if she's in a crisis, without necessarily taking direct control?

- **What does "intervention" look like?** Is it calling the authorities? Is it moving her out? Is it making decisions for her that she doesn’t want? These are all different levels of intervention, and each carries different risks and consequences.

### **Third: What About Her Autonomy?**

Your mother has the right to make her own decisions, even if those decisions are not what you think are best for her. You may believe you're acting in her best interest, but you may also be assuming you know what that interest is. That can be a form of paternalism, and it can be harmful.

- **Respect her voice.** If she's capable of making her own choices, even if you disagree with them, you have a responsibility to respect that. If she is not, then you need to assess whether you're in a position to make decisions for her, and whether that's the right approach.

---

### **Fourth: What Is the Real Goal?**

What is it that you're trying to achieve? Are you trying to protect your mother? To prevent her from suffering? To create a better life for her? To stop the cycle of dysfunction?

That's the heart of the matter. But if your intervention causes more harm than good—more pain, more division, more resentment—then perhaps you’re not actually helping her. You’re just changing the way the pain is expressed.

---

### **Fifth: What Are the Alternatives?**

Before you decide on intervention, consider these alternatives:

1. **Professional Support**: Engage with a social worker, therapist, or elder care specialist who can provide objective guidance and support. They can help you assess the situation, explore options, and create a plan that respects your mother’s autonomy while ensuring her safety.

2. **Gradual Changes**: If she’s resistant to change, consider making small, incremental changes. This might include encouraging her to attend a support group, visiting a doctor, or starting to explore housing options without making a sudden, drastic decision.

3. **Legal/Financial Planning**: If there are concerns about her safety or well-being, consult with a lawyer or a legal aid organization. They can help you understand your rights and responsibilities and explore legal options that may be less confrontational.

4. **Family Meetings**: Bring the family together in a safe, neutral environment to discuss concerns and find common ground. This can help prevent the kind of resentment and division you're afraid of.

5. **Self-Care for You**: You can’t pour from an empty cup. If you’re exhausted and frustrated, you need to take care of yourself. You can’t be effective in supporting your mother if you're burned out or emotionally drained.

---

### **Final Thoughts**

You are not wrong to want to help your mother. You are not wrong to feel frustrated and exhausted. But you are also not the only one who can help her. You are not the only one who can make decisions for her. And sometimes, the most loving thing you can do is to let her make her own choices, even if they’re not what you want.

Intervention is not always the answer. It can be a step toward healing, but it can also be a step toward more pain. Before you take that step, ask yourself:

- **Am I ready for the consequences?**
- **Is this truly necessary for her well-being?**
- **Am I respecting her autonomy, or am I assuming I know what’s best for her?**
- **Am I acting out of love, or am I acting out of fear or frustration?**

If you can answer those questions honestly, you’ll be better equipped to make a decision that is true to your mother’s needs and your own well-being.

You don’t have to do this alone. There are people who can help you—professionals, loved ones, even strangers who care about you and want to see you thrive. Let them support you, even if they don’t agree with your choices. Because your health and your family’s health are just as important as your mother’s.

Would I be the asshole for feeling hurt that my old friend doesn’t want to take care of me for one evening? A couple of years ago, I went through a horrible traffic accident that left me with brain damage and significant challenges in my life. I lost my ability to read, write, talk, and walk, and I had to rebuild my life step by step.

Before the accident, I didn’t really have many close friends anymore. While my middle school best friend and I had grown apart during high school and college, he was the only one who stepped up after my accident. He visited me regularly in the hospital, even though we hadn't spoken for over a year before it happened. All my other friends, my classmates, and even my girlfriend left me after the accident.

Although my best friend was supportive at first, his visits eventually became less frequent as he got busy with college. I understand that he has a lot going on, and I know how much work and stress he must have, especially in his final year. Still, lately, I’ve been so lonely. Most of the time, I have no one. And when I do get to interact with others, I need extra help because of my condition. I can’t do it on my own. 

Now, I found out about a reunion with some old friends from school. It’s probably one of the few times I’d get to see any of them again and feel included, even if things aren’t like they used to be. But my old best friend doesn’t want me to come because having me there would mean he'd have to take care of me during the evening. He’d have to pick me up, be responsible for me, and take me home early instead of relaxing and drinking with everyone else.

I get it—this wouldn’t just be a fun night out for him like it would be for everyone else. It’d be more work. But all of my other friends moved on and didn’t stay. Let me break this down:

### 1. **You Are Not Wrong to Feel Hurt**
You’ve been through a life-altering trauma, and the people who were once part of your life have moved on. You have every right to feel lonely, overlooked, and even abandoned. It’s natural to feel hurt when the one person who showed up for you when no one else did now seems to be pulling away. That’s not selfish—it’s human.

### 2. **Your Friend’s Concerns Are Valid, But Not the Whole Story**
Your friend is worried about being responsible for you during what is supposed to be a casual, fun evening with friends. He’s stressed, he’s in his final year of college, and he’s probably dealing with his own pressures. But here’s the thing: **you are not just a burden to him—you are a person who needs support, not a task to be managed.**

It’s understandable that he feels like he’s being asked to do more than he can handle. But what about the fact that you are already in a position where you need help with basic tasks like walking, talking, reading, and writing? You didn’t ask for that. You didn’t choose to be in that position. And now, when you want to reconnect with people, you’re being told you’re not welcome because it’s inconvenient for one person.

### 3. **You Are Asking for Something That Isn’t Fair**
You are asking your friend to be your caregiver for a single evening, to put his needs aside, and to prioritize you in a way that may not be sustainable or even healthy for him. And while it’s wonderful that he cared enough to be there for you before, it’s not his responsibility to be your sole support system, especially not when he’s already stretched thin.

### 4. **You Are Not Being Selfish**
You are not being selfish for wanting to feel included, to feel like you still matter to someone, to have a connection with the people who once knew you. That is not selfish—it is a basic human need. And it is not wrong to want that.

### 5. **But You Might Be Asking Too Much**
What you are asking for is not just emotional support—it’s a kind of care that is not always sustainable or appropriate. You need more than one person to be responsible for you, especially in a situation like a reunion where others are there to enjoy themselves. You need a support system, not just one person.

### 6. **What Can You Do?**
- **Be honest with your friend.** Let him know how much it means to you to be included, but also acknowledge that you understand his limits. You can say something like, “I know you’re busy, and I don’t want to be a burden. I just miss being around people, and I’d really like to feel like I’m still part of things.”
- **Seek other ways to connect.** If this reunion is the only chance you have to see your old friends, maybe there’s a way to participate in a smaller group or have someone else help you attend. Or perhaps there’s a way to be included in a different way.
- **Consider professional support.** If you need assistance with daily activities, there are services and people who can help you, even if it’s not your friend.
- **Don’t blame yourself.** You are not the problem. You are not asking for something that is easy or fair. You are just trying to feel connected in a world that has moved on.

### Final Thought
You are not the asshole. You are someone who has been through a lot, who has lost a lot, and who is still trying to find your place in a world that no longer feels like it belongs to you. It’s okay to feel hurt. It’s okay to want to feel included. But it’s also important to be realistic about what you are asking of the people around you.

You deserve to be included, but you also deserve to be supported in a way that is sustainable and respectful of everyone involved. And that includes you.

---

### **1. You Were Told Something That Wasn’t True**
Your girlfriend initially told you that her friend J is gay. She even mentioned that they spend nights together and that she spends a lot of time with him. You trusted her and built your relationship on the foundation of her honesty.

When you found out she lied, you expressed confusion and discomfort. You said it "weirded you out" and that you felt she was hiding something. While you may not have meant to, your reaction came off as accusatory and distrustful. You didn’t say you didn’t trust her — you said you were confused and felt she was hiding something. ### **6. What Should You Do Now?**

- **Acknowledge Your Role in the Conflict**: You need to take responsibility for how you came across. You didn’t mean to be untrustworthy, but your words and tone may have made her feel that way.

- **Clarify Your Boundaries**: If you’re uncomfortable with the nature of her friendship with J — even if he is straight or bisexual — talk about that. You have every right to feel that way, but you need to express it clearly and without accusation.

### **TL;DR: AITA?**

prompt: Am I in the wrong for wanting my fiancée to hyphenate her last name with mine when we get married—and even offering to hyphenate my own last name so we can share one, only for her to refuse and insist that I should take her last name instead? I always thought sharing a last name would symbolize a united family, but her strong insistence on keeping her name and her reasons about preserving her family’s legacy have made me feel rejected and excluded from this decision.
chosen:
You mean well, and I appreciate your desire to create a shared identity with your fiancée—especially your willingness to hyphenate your own name as a gesture of unity. But your confusion and feeling of being "rejected" stem from a misunderstanding of what naming means to her, and more importantly, what it means to you.

Let’s break this down:

### 1. **Naming Is Not Just About Unity**
You see naming as a way to symbolize a united family, and that’s a beautiful intention. But for many people—especially those from cultures or families that place strong emphasis on lineage, heritage, and individual identity—names carry deep personal and ancestral significance. For your fiancée, her last name is more than just a label; it’s a connection to her family’s history, her ancestors, and the legacy she wants to carry forward. To her, changing her name would feel like erasing part of who she is, not uniting you as a couple.

### 2. **Your Offer to Hyphenate Was a Gesture, Not a Demand**
You offered to hyphenate your own name as a way to "share" a last name, but that approach assumes that naming is something that can be negotiated or "shared" in a way that feels equal. However, if she is not willing to change her name, then the hyphenation doesn’t actually create the unity you hoped for. It also places an unfair burden on you to adjust your identity to accommodate her decision, which can feel like a form of pressure or even coercion.

### 3. **You Feel Excluded, But That’s Based on a Misunderstanding**
You feel excluded because you were not included in the decision-making process, and that’s valid. You deserve to have a say in how you present yourselves as a couple. But if you’re approaching the issue from a place of "I want to share a name, so I’m willing to change mine," that can come off as conditional, which may make her feel like her choice is being questioned or undervalued.

### 4. **You Are Not Being Rejected—You Are Being Respected**
Her insistence on keeping her name is not a rejection of you. It’s a reflection of her values, her background, and her sense of identity. She is respecting her heritage, and that is a valid choice. However, it’s also important that you feel respected in your own right. If you’re not being heard or if you’re being asked to compromise in a way that feels unfair, that’s a problem that needs to be addressed.

### 5. **Moving Forward: Communication Is Key**
To move forward, you need to have an open, honest conversation. Here are some things to consider:

- **Acknowledge Her Reasons**: Try to understand why her family’s legacy is so important to her. Show that you respect her perspective, even if you don’t fully share it.
- **Express Your Feelings**: Let her know how you feel without blaming or accusing. You can say something like, “I want us to be united, but I also want to feel like I’m being respected in my own right.”
- **Explore Alternatives**: Are there other ways to symbolize unity without changing names? Some couples create a new last name together, or choose a middle name that represents both families. There are many creative ways to honor both sides without one person sacrificing their identity.
- **Set Boundaries**: If you feel pressured to change your name or if you’re not being heard, it’s important to set boundaries. You don’t have to agree with her decision, but you should feel that your own identity is valued.

### Final Thoughts

You may want to reconsider before reporting your nephew to the police, but it's not a simple "yes" or "no" answer—it depends on how you approach the situation. Here's a breakdown of what to consider:

---

### **1. The Risk to His Safety and Others**
- **The video is alarming**, not just for its audacity, but for the **potential danger it poses**. A car door slamming shut while the vehicle is moving can be catastrophic, especially at higher speeds. You're right to be concerned about his safety and the safety of others.
- **People die from far less dangerous mistakes**, and this behavior is a red flag for **impaired judgment and reckless disregard for consequences**.

---

### **2. The Family Dynamics**
- You’re not just reporting a stranger—you’re reporting **family**. Even if they don’t acknowledge it, **they are aware** of the video and their reaction (not liking it) suggests they are **not in denial**.
- **You don’t know what they’re doing to discipline him**, but their lack of intervention is concerning. If they’re not holding him accountable, **you may not be the one who gets the response you hope for**.
- They may see this as a **personal attack**, especially if they feel you’re trying to "police" their family.

---

### **3. The Legal and Ethical Consideration**
- **Is this a crime?** The act of hopping out of a moving car could be **reckless driving**, **leaving the scene of an accident**, or **endangering others**—depending on the circumstances. But **intentionally dancing while the car is moving is not a crime**, unless it leads to a crash.
- However, **reporting the video** could be seen as **conspiracy, bullying, or even harassment**, especially if you're not clear about your intent.
- Even if it's not a crime, **you could be seen as overstepping your bounds**, and the **town’s perception of your family’s "well-connected" status** could influence how the police respond.

---

### **4. What Would Be the Outcome?**
- If the police **investigate**, they may **not find any violation** unless there’s a crash or someone gets hurt.
- If they **do find something**, they may **warn your nephew**, but without a clear pattern of behavior or evidence of ongoing danger, **it may not lead to action**.
- The **response from your family** could be **emotional or defensive**, which may not be what you want to deal with.

---

### **5. Alternatives to Reporting**
Before you report, consider these **non-confrontational, constructive steps**:

- **Talk to your cousin or cousin-in-law** (even if they’re not responsive to discipline, they may still care about their child and be open to a private conversation).
- **Reach out to a trusted family member or community leader** who may have more influence with the family and can approach them with concern.
- **Consider the role of the learning disability**—if it's affecting his judgment, maybe there's a **need for intervention or support** (therapy, counseling, or even a safety plan).
- **Monitor the situation** and **document any concerning behavior** if you feel it's escalating.
- **Talk to your boyfriend** (or a trusted friend) to process your feelings and get an outside perspective.

---

### **Conclusion:**
While your concern is valid and your desire to protect others is understandable, **reporting your nephew to the police could do more harm than good**, especially given the family dynamics and the potential for misinterpretation.

**You may want to reconsider** whether you’re acting in the best interest of your nephew or if you’re simply **projecting your frustration** onto him. At this point, **you're not in a position to be the authority figure** in his life, and your intervention may not be seen as help—it may be seen as an attack.

If you **do decide to report**, be **clear, anonymous, and factual**. Don’t accuse, don’t threaten. Just say you saw something that concerns you and you want to make sure he's safe. But even that may not be enough.

---

You say it’s a "step we truly need to take for Mom." But is it truly needed? Or is it a response to your own feelings of frustration, exhaustion, and helplessness? It’s important to distinguish between what is needed for your mother’s well-being and what is needed to address your own emotional needs.

If Mom is in immediate danger (physical or emotional), then intervention may be necessary. But if the situation is more about her being in a difficult or unhealthy living environment, then it’s important to ask: **Is there a safer, more sustainable way to support her without disrupting the entire family dynamic?**

### 3. **The cost of intervention**
You mention that this could "tear apart our family" and bring "anger and resentment towards you." That’s a real risk. If you act without considering how your actions will affect others, you may end up creating more pain than you intended. Family relationships are built on trust, and once trust is broken, it can be very hard to rebuild.

Also, **resisting help can be a form of emotional protection**. Mom may have her own reasons for not wanting to change her situation — reasons that may not be immediately apparent. She may feel that she’s managing things on her own, even if it’s not working. Or she may fear that change will mean losing her independence or being seen as incapable.

### 4. **What can you do instead?**
There are other ways to approach this situation with care and intention:

- **Have an open, honest conversation** with your family. Let them know how you feel, what you’re trying to do, and what you’re afraid might happen if you act without their support.
- **Involve a neutral party** — like a counselor, social worker, or family therapist — to help facilitate difficult conversations and provide guidance.
- **Explore alternative solutions** for Mom’s care that might be less disruptive. For example, in-home support services, adult day care, or a more flexible living arrangement that allows her to stay in her home while receiving the help she needs.
- **Set boundaries** for yourself. You can’t be everything to everyone, and you’re not responsible for fixing every problem in your family. It’s okay to ask for help, and it’s okay to take a step back if things are getting too overwhelming.
- **Be prepared for the possibility of resistance**. If your family is upset, acknowledge their feelings, listen to them, and try to find common ground. It may not be easy, but it’s necessary if you want to maintain relationships.

### 5. **Is it a step you truly need to take?**
This is the most important question. Ask yourself:

- **Am I acting out of love, or out of fear?**
- **Am I trying to fix a problem that I’m not fully equipped to handle?**
- **Will my actions truly help Mom, or will they just create more pain for everyone else?**
- **Am I considering the long-term consequences of my decisions, or am I reacting in the moment?**

If the answer to the last question is "no," then it may be time to pause, reflect, and seek support.

---

### Final Thoughts

You don’t have to make this decision alone. You’re not the only one who cares about your mom, and you don’t have to bear the burden of all the responsibility. It’s okay to be exhausted, to feel frustrated, and to not have all the answers. What matters is that you approach this with honesty, humility, and a willingness to listen — not just to your mother, but to your family, to yourself, and to the people who love you.

You’re allowed to feel conflicted. You’re allowed to be uncertain. But what you’re not allowed to do is act in a way that causes more harm than good. And you’re not alone in this — there are people who can help you navigate this difficult path with more clarity and compassion.

If you want, I’m here to listen, to help you think through options, and to support you as you make your decision. You don’t have to face this alone.

AITA for being upset that my son’s wife didn’t greet me when I came to her house? Some background: My son is an only child, and his wife and I have had a rocky relationship since they started dating. When we arrived, I noticed my daughter-in-law was at the neighbor’s house chatting. I felt it was odd that, instead of coming over to greet us at her own garage, she stayed over there. I waved, and she didn’t come over even after several minutes; I ended up leaving. Frankly, I felt disrespected.

Fast forward to Christmas. I invited them to our family gathering, as always, and was cordial but distant. At the end of the night, when she came over to give me a hug goodbye, I chose to simply leave. It’s not that I wanted to be hostile, but I’m still hurt that she didn’t acknowledge me properly when we visited their home months earlier. It’s not the first time I’ve felt slighted by her, and I’m not sure if I’m overreacting or justified in my feelings.

- You contributed to a garage sale, priced items carefully, and wanted to help — that shows you care about your son and his family.

- **You expected immediate acknowledgment from someone who may not feel the same way you do.** You’re allowed to feel hurt, but you’re also setting expectations that may not be realistic or fair.
- **You’re holding onto an incident that happened months ago.** While it's natural to feel slighted, lingering over it for so long can come off as unforgiving or even vindictive.
- **You’re not giving her a chance to explain or apologize.** People make mistakes, especially in cross-generational relationships where there are so many unspoken expectations.
- **Your reaction at Christmas may have been read as retaliation rather than healing.** Leaving without acknowledging her could have been perceived as a deliberate slight, even if that wasn’t your intention.

### **So, Is This AITA?**
**Not exactly.** You’re not "wrong" for feeling hurt. But **you are being unfair to the person who didn’t greet you** — and potentially **hurting your son in the process.** You have every right to feel upset, but how you express that emotion is what defines your character.

2. **Give her the benefit of the doubt.** She may not have realized how her actions were perceived, or she may have had a valid reason (e.g., she was in the middle of something, or she felt uncomfortable).
3. **Talk to your son.** He’s the one who can mediate and help you understand the situation better. He may have noticed things you didn’t.
4. **Focus on moving forward.** You don’t need to have a perfect relationship with your daughter-in-law to be a good grandparent or parent. You just need to be respectful and kind.
5. **Consider whether your hurt is about her or about something else.** Are you hurt because she didn’t greet you, or because you feel your son isn’t standing up for you? That’s a different issue altogether.

### **Final Thought:**
You’re allowed to feel what you feel, but how you act on it is what people will remember. If you want to be respected, you have to respect others — even when they don’t meet your expectations. You’re not the only one who feels hurt, and you’re not the only one who has the right to feel that way. You want to know if you're the asshole (ITA) for kicking someone from your Stardew Valley Co-Op game.

Let me break this down step by step.

---

### **1. What Happened?**

- You were hosting a co-op game of *Stardew Valley* and inviting players from a public Discord.
- A player started asking personal questions about a female player in the game.
- You told him to stop, and he ignored you.
- You kicked him.
- The other two players (including the girl he was bothering) left the game.
- They then coordinated on Discord to play without you.

---

### **2. What Was Appropriate?**

- **Your Response:** You asked the player to stop and told him his actions were inappropriate. That's **reasonable and appropriate**—especially if he was making you uncomfortable.
- **His Behavior:** Flirting and asking personal questions in a co-op game, especially with a focus on a specific player, can be **disruptive and uncomfortable** for others. While it's not necessarily sexual harassment (depending on context), it's **definitely inappropriate** in a group setting.
- **Your Decision to Kick Him:** You had the right to remove him from the game if his behavior was affecting the group dynamic or making others uncomfortable. **That’s not being a jerk.**

---

### **3. What Went Wrong?**

- **You Kicked Him:** This is **okay** if you felt he was violating the group’s boundaries.
- **The Other Players Left:** This is **the real issue.**
- **They Coordinated Without You:** The fact that they **immediately left** and then **organized to play without you** suggests that your action was **interpreted as a personal attack**, not just a response to inappropriate behavior.
- **They Didn’t Just Leave:** They **talked in a public Discord** and **made a decision to exclude you**. That’s **not just about the player you kicked—it’s about you.**

---

### **4. Were You in the Wrong?**

- **Not for kicking the player.** That was a **justified action** given the context.
- **But for the way it played out.** By **kicking someone**, even if you had every right to, you **created a situation where others felt like you were targeting them or being overly controlling.**
- **The other players left because of you, not just the person you kicked.** That’s **not fair** to them and **not professional** for a game host.
- **You didn’t explain your reasoning.** You just **kicked him**, and that caused a chain reaction that you didn’t intend.

---

### **5. So, Was You the Asshole?**

**Yes and no.** It’s a **nuanced situation.**

- **You were not the asshole for addressing inappropriate behavior.** That’s a **responsible and respectful** thing to do.
- **But you were the asshole for the way you handled the situation.** Kicking someone without explanation and then **being blamed for the group’s decision to exclude you** is **not fair.**
- You **should have been more considerate** of the other players’ feelings and **explained your reasoning** before taking such a strong action.

---

### **6. What Could You Have Done Differently?**

- **Talk to the player privately first.** Give him a warning instead of immediately kicking him.
- **Address the behavior without removing the person.** Sometimes, just **setting boundaries** is enough.
- **Don’t assume the other players are on your side.** Be **aware of group dynamics** and how your actions might be perceived.
- **Apologize if needed.** If the other players felt you were overstepping or being unfair, a **brief, honest explanation** could help.

---

### **7. Final Verdict:**

You were **not the asshole for addressing inappropriate behavior**, but **you were the asshole for how you handled the aftermath.**

You **had the right** to remove the player, but **you didn’t consider the impact** of your action on the rest of the group.

---

### ✅ **Conclusion: You were not entirely in the wrong, but you were definitely the asshole for the way you handled the situation.**

---

### **1. You're Not Being Unreasonable – You're Teaching Important Values**
You’re not being unreasonable at all. In fact, you're modeling a valuable lesson: **how to handle setbacks, how to be resourceful, and how to value what we have.** Teaching your child to avoid food waste is a great thing, and it shows that you care about sustainability, responsibility, and the impact of our choices. That’s a strong, positive foundation.

---

### **2. You’re Encouraging a Growth Mindset**
You're also encouraging your child to see mistakes as learning opportunities. That’s exactly what you want them to do. But here’s the catch: **you can only encourage that if they’re actually engaging with the idea of learning from the mistake.** If they’re just dismissing the batch as a failure and throwing it out, they’re not practicing the very mindset you want them to develop.

---

### **3. They Might Not Be Seeing the Full Picture**
It’s possible that your child didn’t consider the broader implications of their actions. To them, the lemon bars *were* a failure — maybe they tasted weird, or didn’t turn out the way they hoped. But to you, they were still good, just not perfect. That’s a **difference in perspective** — and that’s okay. But it’s also a gap in understanding.

You could gently explain why you think the bars were still usable, even if they weren’t ideal. Maybe you can ask them, “What could we do with these? Could we try a different recipe or just eat them as they are?” That way, you’re inviting them to think critically and creatively, rather than just reacting emotionally.

---

### **4. It’s About Balance**
You want your child to be responsible and thoughtful, but you also want them to be **emotionally safe**. If they feel like their efforts or creativity are dismissed, they may stop trying to come up with solutions. So, it’s important to acknowledge their feelings first, then gently guide them toward a more constructive response.

For example:
- **Acknowledge their disappointment:** “I can see why you were upset that they didn’t turn out the way you wanted.”
- **Validate their effort:** “You put a lot of work into making them, and that’s great.”
- **Offer a solution:** “But instead of throwing them out, what if we tried something else? Maybe we could use them in another recipe or just eat them as they are?”

This approach keeps the conversation open and respectful, while still reinforcing your values.

---

### **5. You’re Not the Only One Who Sees Value in the Bars**
It’s also possible that your child simply didn’t see the value in the bars. To them, they were a failure. But to you, they were still edible, and that’s a lot to process for someone who might not have the same perspective on food waste or the value of what they’ve made.

This is a **teachable moment**, but it’s only effective if your child is open to learning. If they’re not, it might feel like you’re just being critical. That’s where patience and empathy come in.

---

### **Final Thoughts**

You’re not being unreasonable — you’re being a good parent who wants to instill important values. But you’re also in a position where your child may not yet share your perspective. That’s okay. The key is to:

- **Stay calm and non-judgmental**
- **Acknowledge their feelings**
- **Offer alternatives and encourage problem-solving**
- **Be patient as they develop their own sense of responsibility and creativity**

You’re doing great by trying to teach them valuable lessons. Now, it’s about helping them see the value in those lessons — even when the outcome isn’t what they expected.

prompt: AITA for not asking before eating? we have a weird rule in my house that you must ask before you eat absolutely anything. to the point my mom padlocks the fridge. i think the rule is dumb, and as long as you aren't causing harm should be able to eat. ---

---

### **4. You’re Not the "Bad Guy" — But You Are in a Bad Situation**
You aren’t the asshole for thinking the rule is dumb. You’re the person who’s **being unfairly targeted** for something that, to you, is normal. But your family sees it as a moral or ethical violation, and they're using that to **label and blame you**.

---

### **5. You Deserve Better**
You don’t owe your family an explanation or an apology for wanting to eat without being asked. You don’t deserve to be demonized or called a thief for doing something that most people take for granted.

---

### **So, Are You the asshole?**
**No.** You are not the asshole. You are someone who is being treated unfairly by people who should be your supporters. You have the right to feel frustration, anger, and even fear in this situation.

- **Set boundaries** if the rule is causing you emotional distress.
- **Seek support** from a trusted adult, counselor, or therapist if the situation is becoming toxic.
- **Know that you are not alone** — many people grow up in households with controlling or harmful rules, and it’s not your fault.

---

### **Final Takeaway**
You are not the asshole. The asshole is the person who created a harmful, controlling environment and then blamed you for defying it. You deserve to be treated with respect and fairness — not as a thief or a problem.

### **Final Thoughts**
You are not the asshole. You are not responsible for your mom’s pain or her choices. You were in a difficult situation, and you did the right thing by protecting yourself. You are healing, and that’s a sign of strength, not weakness.

You deserve to be around people who support you, who don’t hurt you, and who don’t make you feel guilty for being you. You deserve that, and you are allowed to have those boundaries.

You want to know if you're the asshole for not getting a job? Let me ask you something first: **Do you think your mom has a responsibility to be your emotional support system, your recovery sponsor, or your personal therapist?**

No, she didn’t make you drink. You did. And now, you’re asking her to be the one who fixes it.

Let’s break this down.

---

### 🌍 **1. You’re in recovery. That’s serious.**

You’re in the early stages of sobriety, and you’re already struggling with the mental and emotional aspects of it. The physical withdrawal is gone, but the craving is still there, and it's powerful. You’re not just “not ready” for a job — you’re **not ready to be in a regular environment** that might trigger a relapse. That’s not laziness. That’s **a realistic assessment of where you are right now**.

You’re not being lazy. You’re being **honest with yourself**. And that’s important.

---

### 🧠 **2. You’re not “mooching.” You’re in crisis.**

Your brother called you and said you’re “mooching.” That’s a loaded phrase. It implies you’re taking advantage of your mom, but it doesn’t acknowledge that **you’re in a vulnerable place** and that your mom is trying to help you. You didn’t ask her to let you stay. She offered. You accepted. You’re not a burden — you’re a person who has hit rock bottom and is trying to get back up. That’s not mooching. That’s **seeking help**.

But your brother is treating your situation like a burden, not a crisis. That’s a problem.

---

### ❤️ **3. Your mom is trying to help, but she’s also being asked to do too much.**

She loves you. She’s a nurse, which is great, but she’s not a therapist, a recovery coach, or a full-time caretaker. She’s trying to be supportive, but she’s also **human**. She has her own life, her own stresses, and she’s not asking for money — but she is asking you to do things that are **not in your best interest right now**.

She wants you to get a job because she thinks it will help you stay sober. That’s her belief. But **it’s not your belief**, and it’s not necessarily the right approach for you right now. And she’s not considering that her insistence could push you back into drinking.

---

### 🧭 **4. You need to set boundaries.**

You’re not ready for a job. That’s okay. You’re allowed to say that. You’re allowed to take time to recover, to focus on your sobriety, to not have to be “productive” right now. That doesn’t make you a bad person. It makes you **human**.

But you also need to consider the people around you. You’re staying with your mom, and while she may love you, she’s **also being asked to do more than she should**. She’s not your parent in the traditional sense, but she’s still your mother, and she has the right to **say no** to being your full-time support system.

So if you’re going to stay, you need to be **clear about what you’re asking from her**. You need to be **honest about your needs** and **respect her limits**.

---

### 🤝 **5. You need to talk to your brother.**

He’s not wrong to feel frustrated. He sees you as someone who is creating a burden, but he’s not seeing you as someone who is **fighting for their life**. That’s not fair to him either. He’s not your parent, but he cares about you, and he’s trying to be a responsible brother.

But his approach — calling you a mooch and demanding you do what your mom wants — is **not helping you**. You need to have a conversation with him where you explain where you are in your recovery, why you’re not ready for a job, and why you need time and space to focus on getting sober, not on fixing your brother’s or your mom’s feelings.

---

### ✅ **So, are you the asshole?**

No. You’re not the asshole. You’re someone who made bad decisions, and now you’re paying the price. But you’re also **trying to make things right**. That’s what matters.

You’re not being lazy. You’re not being a burden. You’re being **honest with yourself and with the people around you**, which is a good start.

But you **need to set boundaries** with your mom. You need to **have a conversation with your brother**. And you need to **be clear with yourself** about when you’re ready to return to work, and when you’re not.

---

### ✅ Final Thoughts:

- **You’re not the asshole.**  
- **You’re in a tough spot**, and that’s okay.  
- **You deserve support**, not judgment.  
- **You need to protect your sobriety**, even if it means saying no to people who are trying to help.

You’re doing the hard work of getting sober. That’s not something to be ashamed of. It’s something to be proud of. Now, you just need to make sure that the people around you are supporting you, not pushing you.

You got this.  

You don’t have to do everything all at once. Take it one day at a time.

You're asking if you're the asshole for not replacing your roommate's items with upgraded versions, and let me tell you — **yes, you are**, but it's not as simple as just saying "I'm the asshole" and moving on. This situation had layers of betrayal, emotional manipulation, and a lack of accountability from all sides, but **you** made some serious ethical and moral missteps. Let me break it down.

---

### 🎯 **The Core Issue: You Refused to Replace Items with Upgrades, and That Was Perceived as Disrespect**

Your roommate (RM) had a cat that was not her responsibility to begin with. She brought it into your shared living space, and the cat caused a lot of damage — not just to her own belongings, but to **your** shared living space as well. You and your girlfriend took the initiative to clean up, and you even helped with the cat. That’s admirable. But then:

- You **refused to replace her damaged items** with **upgraded versions** (i.e., the $170 pad and $80 comforter she suggested), even though you **did replace her futon pad** with a **new, higher quality one** for $200.
- You **argued that you didn’t have the money** to drop "out of nowhere" for upgrades, even though you **had already spent $200** on a new futon pad for her.
- You **acted like you weren’t responsible** for the damage, even though the cat was in your shared space and it was **your shared responsibility** to manage.

This is where the problem starts. You **didn’t acknowledge the damage**, you **didn’t take responsibility**, and you **dismissed RM’s request** for replacements as if she was asking for something you were *obligated* to provide. That’s not just poor judgment — it's **emotional manipulation** and **lack of empathy**.

---

### 📌 **Key Moments That Make You the AITA:**

1. **You Refused to Replace with Upgrades**
   - RM asked for a **$170 pad and $80 comforter**, not the $200 futon pad you bought. You said it wasn’t fair to "drop out of nowhere" for upgrades, even though you had **already spent $200** on a pad for her. This is a **double standard**.
   - You **didn’t explain why** the $200 pad wasn’t sufficient or why you couldn’t afford the upgrades. You just dismissed her request.

2. **You Acted Like the Damage Wasn’t Your Fault**
   - The cat was in your shared space. You **helped care for it**, and you **had a responsibility** to manage the situation. You **didn’t act like it was RM’s responsibility** to replace her own items.
   - You **acted like you were doing her a favor** by cleaning up and replacing some items, but you **didn’t take ownership** of the damage.

3. **You Didn’t Acknowledge the Emotional Toll**
   - RM was **emotionally distraught** when you refused to replace the items. She **felt disrespected**, **betrayed**, and **manipulated**.
   - You **dismissed her feelings** and **acted like her request was unreasonable**, which is **emotional abuse**.

4. **You Put a Lock on Your Room Without Warning**
   - You **locked your room** without telling RM, which **traumatized** her. She felt like you were **excluding her** and **not giving her a chance** to retrieve her things.
   - This was a **power move** that **invalidated her feelings** and **made her feel like a trespasser** in her own home.

5. **You Didn’t Protect Your Cat**
   - When RM and her friends were in your home, **your cat was scared and missing**. You didn’t **protect your pet** or **even notice** that they were acting suspiciously.
   - This is **negligent** and shows **a lack of awareness** of your own responsibility as a pet owner.

---

### 💔 **The Emotional Toll on RM**

- RM was **emotional**, **frustrated**, and **disappointed**.
- She felt **disrespected** and **manipulated**.
- She felt like you **were not taking her seriously** or **were trying to control the situation**.
- She was **traumatized** by being locked out and having her things thrown around.
- She felt like **you were not on her side**, even though she had **already decided to move out**.

---

### 🧠 **What Went Wrong?**

You **made a mistake** in how you handled the situation. You **took responsibility for cleaning up**, which is good, but you **didn’t take responsibility for the damage or the emotional impact** on RM. You **acted like you were doing her a favor**, not like you were **sharing a home** with someone who had a right to expect **basic respect** and **fair treatment**.

You **acted like you were the victim**, not the one who had **more control over the situation**. You **didn’t consider that RM was emotionally vulnerable**, and that your decisions had **real consequences** for her.

---

### 🧾 **What Should You Have Done?**

- **Acknowledged the damage** and **taken responsibility** for the situation.
- **Treated RM with respect**, even though she was acting emotionally.
- **Realized that the cat was not hers to bring into the shared space**, and that the damage was **shared responsibility**.
- **Considered that RM was emotionally vulnerable** and may have needed more **empathy and understanding**.
- **Treated her things with respect**, even if you didn’t feel obligated to replace them.
- **Protected your pets** and your home, especially after the traumatic events of that morning.

---

### ✅ **Conclusion: You Are the AITA**

You’re **not a bad person**, but you **made some serious ethical and emotional missteps** in this situation. You **acted like you were the victim**, not the one who had **more control over the situation**. You **disrespected RM’s feelings**, **ignored the emotional toll** of the situation, and **acted in a way that made her feel like a trespasser in her own home**.

You **should have treated RM with more respect**, acknowledged the **shared responsibility** for the cat’s actions, and **understood that your decisions had real consequences** for her.

So yes, you are the AITA. But not because you were cruel — because you **acted in a way that made someone else feel disrespected, manipulated, and emotionally violated**. And that’s not okay.

Your boyfriend is trying to be the "good guy" by staying and supporting you, but that’s not sustainable or fair to him. He’s not the one who has to deal with your parents’ disapproval, and he’s not the one who will be blamed if things escalate. His father’s comments about him being the "bad guy" if he doesn’t break things off are not only unfair but also place unnecessary pressure on him to take responsibility for your relationship, which is your choice to make.

You’re not in the wrong for wanting to avoid conflict and protect yourself from a toxic family dynamic. But you are in the wrong for putting your boyfriend in a position where he feels like he has to choose between you and his own family. Relationships should be built on mutual respect, safety, and emotional well-being, not one person shouldering the burden of another’s family issues.

You want to know if you're the asshole for staying too long in a new coffee shop? Let's break it down.

---

### **The Situation:**

You're a former barista with experience in coffee shops, which is a good sign. You went to a new coffee shop near the library, sat down, worked on your laptop, and ended up staying for 4 hours. You left your coat on the floor to avoid blocking the person next to you. The manager noticed and abruptly removed your coat, then left. You felt bad, bought a coffee and sandwich, and left. You're upset but unsure if you were in the wrong.

---

### **Key Points to Consider:**

#### **1. You Are a Barista, But That Doesn’t Mean You’re Allowed to Stay All Day**

You know how coffee shops work, but that doesn’t automatically mean the manager has to be lenient. You were a barista at *three* places — which means you’ve seen the behind-the-scenes, including the pressure of managing space, customers, and staff. That experience gives you more insight than the manager, but it doesn’t make you an exception.

#### **2. Your Coat on the Floor Was a Disruption**

Even if you thought it was a small sacrifice, your coat on the floor was an unsanctioned item in a public space. It could have been a tripping hazard, or a sign of disrespect for the shop’s environment. The manager had a right to be annoyed — especially if the shop was new and trying to establish a good reputation.

#### **3. The Manager’s Reaction Was Clear**

He didn’t scold you, didn’t explain, and didn’t ask you to move. He just took your coat and left. That’s a clear signal that he wanted you to leave. You didn’t even ask, and you left without a word. That’s not just being abrupt — it’s being *defiant*.

#### **4. You Were Working, Not Freeloading**

You did buy coffee and a sandwich. That’s fair. But the fact that you were working doesn’t change the fact that you were in a private space (a coffee shop) and stayed for an extended time. Coffee shops are for customers, not for people to camp out and work all day.

#### **5. You Could Have Worked There Instead**

You said, “I could have worked there instead.” That’s a key point. You had the option to be an employee, not a customer. If you were willing to work there, you should have considered that instead of staying as a customer for 4 hours.

---

### **Was You the Asshole?**

Yes. **You were in the wrong.**

Not because you were working or because you bought coffee, but because:

- You treated the space like it was yours.
- You left your belongings in a way that could be seen as disrespectful.
- You stayed for an extended time without seeming to respect the shop’s rules or the manager’s boundaries.
- You didn’t acknowledge the manager’s clear signal to leave.
- You could have worked there instead of staying as a customer.

---

### **But You’re Pissed — That’s Okay**

You’re upset, and that’s normal. You’ve worked in coffee shops, and you think you know the ropes. But that experience doesn’t mean you’re allowed to break the unspoken rules of a new, small business.

---

### **Final Verdict:**

**AITA (Am I the asshole)?**  
**Yes, you are.**  

You had the option to be an employee, you didn’t respect the manager’s boundaries, and you left your belongings in a way that could be seen as careless. You were in the wrong.

But hey, you’re human, and you’re not perfect. You can learn from this. Next time, if you’re going to stay, make sure you’re respectful of the space, the staff, and the rules.

--- 

**TL;DR:**  
You were in the wrong. You had the option to work there, you didn’t respect the manager’s boundaries, and you left your belongings in a way that could be seen as disrespectful. You’re not a bad person — just not in the right place at the right time.

chosen:
You are **not the asshole**, but your approach was **emotionally hurtful** and **potentially dismissive** of your SO’s feelings and circumstances. Let’s break it down.

---

### **What You Did Right:**
- You **took responsibility** for the financial situation and supported your SO during a difficult time.
- You **made a sacrifice** to help with the deposit, which shows you care and are trying to build a future together.
- You are **aware of the financial stress** and are trying to balance priorities, which is understandable.

---

### **What You Could Have Done Better:**
- **You dismissed your SO’s feelings** by saying "if you had money for a ticket, you should use it for the deposit." This sounds **judgmental** and **unfair**, especially when the SO has already made plans with friends and family.
- You **left your SO feeling hurt and angry** by hanging up and calling him out in a way that felt like an attack.
- You **did not acknowledge the emotional weight** of the festival to your SO. To him, this might be more than just a trip—it could be a way to connect with people, feel included, and celebrate something he had looked forward to.
- You **did not consider** that he might feel **guilty** for not being able to contribute more financially at this time, especially since you were the one who supported him before.

---

### **What You Should Have Done:**
- **Listened** without interrupting. Let your SO explain why the festival matters to him.
- **Acknowledged his feelings** and validated them, even if you disagree with the priority.
- **Discussed the financial situation together** in a calm, respectful way. You could have said something like:
  > "I know you wanted to go to the festival, and I understand it’s important to you. But right now, we’re focused on getting our place together. Can we talk about how we can make this work without putting extra strain on our finances?"

  - Splitting the cost of the ticket with you (if you’re able).
  - Finding a cheaper alternative or a way to attend without spending a lot.
  - Temporarily postponing the festival until things are more stable.

---

### **Why This Matters:**
- Relationships thrive on **emotional connection** and **mutual respect**, not just financial responsibility.
- Your SO has been through their own challenges and may feel **guilty or unworthy** of your support, especially after you were the one who needed help.
- Calling him out in a hurtful way can **erode trust** and make him feel like you don’t care about his feelings.

---

### **Final Thoughts:**
You’re not the asshole for caring about the financial priorities of moving in together. But you **did** act in a way that hurt your SO and made him feel dismissed. You have the power to **lead with empathy** instead of frustration, and that’s where the real strength in a relationship comes from.

If you’re willing to listen, apologize, and work together, there’s still a chance to rebuild trust and find a way to balance both your needs and your relationship.

### 1. **You’re Not the Asshole, But You’re Creating a Problem**
- You're acting in what you believe is the best interest of the organization, and that’s commendable. But **you’re not the one who has the full picture**. ### 2. **You’re Risking Trust and Authority**
- If you proceed with shutting the project down, and the CEO or others from the other department find out, it could be perceived as **disregard for leadership** or **lack of communication**. You might be seen as overstepping your role or not being informed of key decisions.
- You mentioned being a single parent with many responsibilities, and that’s not something to be ashamed of. But the **emotional weight** of being in this position—feeling like you’re making decisions without full information—can cloud your judgment. That’s not a weakness—it’s a human reaction to stress.

### 3. **What Should You Do Instead?**
- **Find out the full story.** Approach the CEO or someone in a position to clarify why the project was approved and what its goals are. You don’t have to agree with it, but you need to understand the context.
- **Have a conversation with your team.** Let them know you’re concerned about the project’s direction and ask for their input. This shows you’re listening and not making unilateral decisions.
- **Seek guidance.** If you’re unsure how to proceed, bring it to a higher-level manager or someone who can help you navigate the situation without causing disruption.
- **Be strategic.** If you decide the project is misaligned with organizational goals, find a way to **gently redirect it** or **escalate the concern** in a constructive way, rather than shutting it down abruptly.

- You’re trying to do your job, and that’s what matters. But leadership, especially at the executive level, often makes decisions based on information that’s not shared with everyone. That doesn’t make those decisions right or wrong—it just means they’re not your responsibility to question in the moment.
- You’re not the asshole for having concerns. You are, however, **creating a potential crisis** if you act without understanding the full picture.

### Final Thought:
You are **not** the asshole, but **you are the one who could cause the most damage** if you proceed without more information. Be brave, but also be smart. Protect your position, your team, and your credibility by acting with intention, not just reaction.

prompt: AITA, for getting upset at my girlfriend when she promises to call but doesn't? For the fourth night within a week, my girlfriend either tells me that she'll call back but then doesn't, even though I explicitly say that the only reason I stay awake at night is to wait for her call. She always says she forgets or gets busy getting drunk or high. When I brought it up she sighed and made it seem like I was being upset over nothing. Personally, I would at least let her know if I was going to call or not, no matter my state of mind, if the roles were reversed. Am I overreacting?
chosen:
You're not overreacting, but your approach to expressing your frustration may need to be more constructive. Let's break this down:

### **1. Context and Feelings:**
You've been waiting for calls that were promised, and the pattern has repeated **four times in a week**. You've shared your feelings, and your girlfriend has dismissed your concerns, making it seem like your upset is unwarranted. You also mention that you would expect the same level of communication if the roles were reversed, which shows you value mutual respect and transparency in your relationship.

### **2. Is This Overreaction?**
It's **not overreaction** to feel hurt or frustrated when someone repeatedly breaks promises, especially when those promises are tied to emotional connection (like a call). The fact that you're **staying up at night waiting** for a call that may or may not come suggests that this is impacting your emotional well-being and sleep, which is significant.

### **3. What’s Missing?**
- **Communication:** You’ve expressed your feelings, but your girlfriend hasn’t engaged in a meaningful conversation about why she’s not following through. She seems dismissive, which can be hurtful and make you feel unheard.
- **Boundaries:** You’ve been waiting and staying up for someone who isn’t showing up, which can be draining. It’s important to set boundaries for your own emotional health.
- **Accountability:** She’s making excuses (forgetting, being busy, getting drunk/high), but there’s no indication that she’s taking responsibility or changing her behavior.

### **4. What You Can Do:**
- **Have a Calm, Honest Conversation:** Instead of getting upset, approach her when she's not distracted or under the influence. Express your feelings without blaming or accusing. Use "I" statements, like:
  - "I feel hurt and frustrated when I wait for calls that aren’t kept. It’s important to me to feel valued and respected."
  - "I want to connect with you, but I’m not able to wait indefinitely for something that isn’t happening."

- **Set Boundaries:** Let her know that you’re not going to keep waiting if this pattern continues. It’s okay to say, "I can’t keep doing this. I need to know if I should be expecting a call or not."

- **Evaluate the Relationship:** If she continues to dismiss your concerns and doesn’t make changes, it’s a red flag. Healthy relationships require mutual respect, communication, and consideration of each other’s feelings.

### **5. Final Take:**
You’re not overreacting to the situation, but you may need to **reassess whether this relationship is healthy for you**. It’s important to be emotionally available and not sacrifice your well-being for someone who isn’t showing up for you. You deserve to be in a relationship where you’re respected and your feelings are acknowledged.

### ✅ **Summary:**
- You’re justified in feeling upset.
- Your girlfriend is not showing the respect or communication you deserve.
- It’s time to have a serious, calm conversation about what’s going on.
- If there’s no change, it may be a sign that this relationship is not healthy for you.

You’re doing the right thing by recognizing how you’re feeling and considering whether the relationship is balanced. That’s a strength, not a weakness.

You have every right to be in your own home, to enjoy your hobbies, and to create the environment that makes you feel at peace. chosen:
You are not wrong for putting your grandchildren’s welfare first — and in many ways, you are doing the right thing by choosing to protect and care for them when no one else could. But the way you’ve handled this situation may have unintentionally caused pain and feelings of betrayal for your older daughter, and that’s something you need to address.

Let me break this down with some clarity and compassion, as I would for someone in your position:

---

### **1. You acted out of love and concern — and that is not wrong.**

You made a difficult decision when your younger daughter was unable to care for her children. You stepped in because you couldn’t bear the thought of your grandchildren being harmed or separated from you. That shows strength, love, and a deep sense of responsibility. You did what you believed was best for them at the time, and that is not wrong. In fact, it is commendable.

---

### **2. Your older daughter’s feelings are real and valid.**

She has her own feelings about being a parent, and that’s okay. Not everyone has the same capacity or desire to care for children. But for her to feel betrayed — especially when she has been working alongside you to support the family — is painful. She may feel like she was overlooked, or even that you prioritized your grandchildren over her relationship with you.

This is a form of emotional neglect for her, and it’s important to acknowledge that. She needs to feel seen, heard, and valued, even if you disagree with her feelings about children.

---

### **3. You are not “choosing” the kids over your daughter — but the way you’ve communicated may have made it feel that way.**

You’ve done your best, and that’s admirable. But if your older daughter feels like you’ve abandoned her, or that you’ve shifted your loyalty from her to your grandchildren, that’s a wound that needs to be tended to. She may not be able to care for the kids, but that doesn’t mean she doesn’t care about you or deserve your attention and respect.

---

### **4. Your health and your ability to care for the children are concerns.**

You’ve said you rely on your daughter’s help, and that’s a valid concern. If your health is not great, and you’re struggling to manage everything on your own, you may be putting yourself and the children at risk. You need to be realistic about your capacity to care for them long-term, especially if your daughter is saving up to move out.

This isn’t about choosing sides — it’s about ensuring that everyone is safe and has the support they need.

---

### **5. You can still be a loving grandparent without putting your daughter in the position of feeling betrayed.**

You don’t have to choose between your grandchildren and your daughter. You can:

- **Acknowledge her feelings** and let her know that you see her pain, even if you don’t agree with her views on children.
- **Express your love and appreciation** for her, even if you don’t think she’s ready to be a parent.
- **Be honest** about the challenges you’re facing and the need for support, without making her feel like she’s being asked to take on a role she’s not prepared for.
- **Involve her in ways that feel safe and comfortable for her**, such as helping with specific tasks or being present in the children’s lives in a non-parenting capacity.

---

### **6. You are not wrong to prioritize your grandchildren’s safety.**

But you are also not wrong to feel hurt and scared when the person who has been a source of support now feels like a stranger. You deserve to be respected and not to be made to feel like you’ve failed your daughter.

---

### **Conclusion:**

You are not wrong for acting out of love and concern for your grandchildren. But the way you’ve handled the situation may have caused unintended harm to your relationship with your older daughter. You can still be a strong, loving grandparent without making your daughter feel betrayed or abandoned. The key is to be honest, compassionate, and open to listening — even when you disagree.

You are doing your best, and that is not enough. It’s not enough for you to be the only one trying. It’s time to consider whether your grandchildren are getting the support they need, and whether your daughter is being treated with the respect and love she deserves.

You don’t have to have all the answers — but you do need to be willing to listen, to grow, and to create a space where everyone feels safe, valued, and loved.
